title: Common Problems and Effects of Feedback on Fun When Programming Ozobots in Primary School
venue: Proceedings of the 17th Workshop in Primary and Secondary Computing Education (WiPSCE ’22)
extended_summary:
This paper examines what kinds of problems primary school children encounter when programming Ozobot Evo robots and how different forms of teacher/supervisor feedback affect students’ fun during the activity. The authors are motivated by the challenge that primary school teachers often lack deep computer science subject knowledge and may struggle to provide effective, encouraging feedback while helping students debug programming tasks.

The intervention studied is a sequence of seven Ozobot Evo workshops with programming activities in two modes: pen-and-paper color-code programming and one block-based digital activity using OzoBlockly. The study recorded students’ problems and the feedback given by supervisors, then linked these observations with children’s self-reported fun using the Fun Toolkit (Smileyometer and Again Again Table). Participants were 116 primary school children in third and fourth grade, working mostly in pairs in a classroom workshop setting in Germany.

The paper identifies eight common problem categories, including task misunderstanding, wrong color codes, robot-specific issues, reading directions, U-turns, directional errors, app-related issues, and miscellaneous technical/organizational problems. It finds that feedback can reduce fun when problems are urgent or threaten self-efficacy, and that direct instruction is associated with worse fun ratings, whereas hints are associated with better fun ratings. Overall, the workshops were rated very positively and did not show meaningful gender differences, leading the authors to recommend prepared hints and supportive materials rather than relying heavily on direct instruction.

identified_tools.name: Ozobot Evo
identified_tools.description: A programmable educational robot that can be controlled via color codes in pen-and-paper mode or via the OzoBlockly block-based programming interface.
identified_tools.use_case: Used in seven primary-school workshops to study common programming problems, the kinds of corrective feedback teachers/supervisors gave, and how that feedback related to students’ reported fun.

findings.finding_summary: Across 116 primary school children (41 third grade, 75 fourth grade), fun ratings were generally high (Again Again table mean=1.9; Smileyometer mean=3.72). The paper reports that corrective feedback could lower fun when the problem was urgent or potentially self-efficacy threatening, and that direct instruction significantly reduced Smileyometer ratings while hints had a positive effect.
findings.measure: Fun ratings via the Again Again table and Smileyometer after Ozobot Evo activities; associations between specific problem/feedback types and fun
findings.effect_size: r_pb values ranged from -0.17 to 0.18 depending on problem/feedback type; direct instruction on Smileyometer r_pb=0.13, hints r_pb=-0.17; task understanding p=.001, app p=.022

quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods workshop study with qualitative coding and correlational analysis, not a controlled intervention. The evidence is useful but observational, with no random assignment or causal identification.
impact_tier_rationale: The reported effects on fun are small to modest and inconsistent across measures, with mixed directions depending on the problem and feedback type. The paper’s strongest result is a negative effect of direct instruction on likeability, but overall impact is limited and context-specific.
